title: How loud is too loud: sound levels of everyday sounds and WHO safe weekly listening times

sources.title: Deafness and hearing loss: Safe listening (Questions and answers)

facts.text: WHO estimates that more than 1 billion young adults are at risk of permanent hearing loss that could be avoided, because of unsafe listening.
Sound level is measured in decibels (dB).
Typical levels: a library is about 40 dB and a normal conversation about 60 dB.
Typical levels: a doorbell 80 dB, heavy traffic heard inside a car 85 dB, a shouted conversation 90 dB, a motorcycle 95 dB, a hair dryer 100 dB, standing near a siren 120 dB.
Safe listening time per week: 60 dB or less has no limit; 80 dB 40 hours; 85 dB 12 hours 30 minutes; 90 dB 4 hours.
Safe listening time per week: 95 dB 1 hour 15 minutes; 100 dB 20 minutes; 120 dB 12 seconds.
WHO says sounds below 80 dB are unlikely to damage hearing.
Even one exposure to an extremely loud sound can damage cells in the inner ear.
Simple check: if you must raise your voice to be heard by someone an arm's length away, the sound is too loud.
WHO advice: keep a device's volume at no more than 60% of its maximum.
WHO advice: well-fitted noise-cancelling headphones help because listeners do not need to raise the volume in noisy places.
WHO advice: wear earplugs in noisy places, and at concerts or other loud events rest the ears in a quiet place for 10 minutes every hour.
Ringing in the ears that does not go away is a warning sign; WHO advises getting a hearing check.

notes: 表格把 WHO 的「常見聲音分貝數」與「每週安全聆聽時間」兩份清單依分貝數併成一張表；數值照原值，不另做換算。
